query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Refining the grain size in the FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coating will enhance its high-temperature wear resistance and promote more uniform (homogeneous) plastic deformation during sliding by increasing the grain boundary area, which facilitates dynamic recrystallization and distributed grain-boundary sliding under thermal activation.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with a baseline (conventionally processed) grain size deposited on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled grain size refinement (using processing methods such as adjusted thermal treatments or deposition parameters) relative to the baseline condition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (temperatures above approximately 500°C, near the service limit of the coating) where thermal activation promotes grain-boundary mediated deformation and dynamic recrystallization.
generation.structural_mediator: The increased density of refined grain boundaries facilitates dynamic recrystallization and enhances grain-boundary sliding, leading to a more homogeneous distribution of deformation and reduction of stress concentration sites.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, refined grains increase the area available for grain boundary sliding and dynamic recrystallization, which distributes the plastic strain more evenly and retards the formation of localized deformation zones that lead to accelerated wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coating, the refined-grain coating will exhibit a lower wear rate and display more uniform (less localized) microscopic plastic deformation during sliding under high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating with its conventional grain size and standard microstructural state.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions (above ~500°C) where thermally activated deformation mechanisms, such as grain-boundary sliding and dynamic recrystallization, are significant.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in wear resistance and the extent of deformation homogenization are uncertain and may depend on precise processing conditions, sliding speeds, and temperature gradients. Further experiments are needed to quantify these effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings on the same conventional metal substrate: one with the baseline grain size and one with a controlled refined grain size achieved by modifying processing parameters. Conduct wear tests under controlled high-temperature sliding conditions (above 500°C) while monitoring the wear rate and mapping the microstructural evolution in the worn zones using microscopic and diffraction techniques.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss or volume loss per unit sliding distance)
Microscopic analysis of deformation features (e.g., via SEM/TEM) to assess the homogeneity of plastic deformation
Grain size distribution before and after sliding
Hardness or microstructural stability measurements at high temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the grain-refined coating does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and fails to show a more homogeneous distribution of plastic deformation (for example, if it develops more localized deformation or cracking compared to the baseline) under the high-temperature sliding conditions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . Keywords: high-entropy alloy (HEA), compositionally complex alloy (CCA), spark plasma sin

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

frame.system: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate
frame.goal: Achieve a mechanistic understanding of how microstructural evolution—such as grain boundary changes, phase transformations, or elemental segregation under high-temperature sliding—governs the overall wear resistance and localized deformation behavior of the coating.
frame.limitation: There is an incomplete understanding of the coupled effects of high-temperature-induced microstructural modifications (e.g., thermally activated slip system changes, dynamic recrystallization, or precipitate evolution) and sliding contact on wear and deformation in the high-entropy coating.
constraints: Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition (e.g., modify grain size or introduce a controlled intermetallic phase)
Predict corresponding directional changes in wear (improvement or degradation) and deformation (more homogeneous vs. localized plasticity)
State the specific high-temperature sliding regime within which the hypothesis is applicable
Identify supporting prior evidence (such as room-temperature studies that indicate a role of microstructural stability or limited high-temperature sliding tests)
Specify a falsifiable result (an experimental outcome that would contradict the hypothesis)
frame.regime: High-temperature sliding conditions, where thermal activation plays a significant role in enabling deformation mechanisms (e.g., at temperatures near the service limit of the coating, typically above 500°C or as appropriate for the intended application)
prior_attempts: Prior studies have investigated the wear resistance of high-entropy alloys at room temperature, linking higher hardness and fine grain sizes with improved performance. However, these approaches fell short by not addressing the thermally activated microstructural changes and deformation mechanisms under high-temperature sliding conditions.
